source.version: Published journal article: Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 2023, 39(5), 40-58; DOI 10.14742/ajet.8923. No separate revision date is stated (PDF pp. 1 and 19, journal header and recommended citation).
source.title_on_document: Effects of a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach on learners’ courseware project performances and perceptions

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is identified in the complete document. The project rubric and all reported quantitative outcome tables are in the main article (PDF pp. 10-13, Tables 1-8); references and publication information complete the PDF (pp. 15-19).

paper_design_summary: Chemistry students in two intact university classes designed PowerPoint courseware during a compulsory course; one class was randomly assigned to ChatGPT-FLGA and the other received traditional flipped learning, with the same teacher and QQ discussion in both groups (PDF pp. 1, 9 and 15). Instructors scored project quality, and questionnaires measured perceptions including creative-thinking tendency (PDF pp. 10-13). Both assessments occurred in week 8 after the assigned learning period, but the exact scored project prompts and ChatGPT access during production of the assessed project are not specified (PDF pp. 6, 9-10).

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of two intact classes was randomly assigned to ChatGPT-FLGA; the other class received T-FLGA. This is class-level allocation within ordinary coursework, not individual student randomization. The author labels the study quasi-experimental; the randomization method is not described (PDF pp. 1 and 9).
assignment.quote: One intact class of 42 students (18 males) was randomly assigned to be the experimental group, which adopted ChatGPT-FLCA.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Participants; corroborated by PDF p. 1 (printed p. 40), abstract. ChatGPT-FLCA is the spelling printed in the quoted Participants sentence.

arms.name: ChatGPT-FLGA
arms.description: Experimental intact class: ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach, including an AI teacher accessed through Tencent QQ, personalized dialogue, assignment reminders and learning-participation feedback. Both classes received flipped instruction and QQ discussions with the same teacher (PDF pp. 1, 5-9).

arms.name: T-FLGA
arms.description: Control intact class: traditional flipped learning guiding approach with instructional resources and QQ discussions, taught by the same teacher, without the ChatGPT-FLGA system (PDF pp. 1 and 9; PDF p. 13, Discussion).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The procedure states that all students completed the post-test; Tables 2-8 retain the class allocation counts of 42 experimental and 39 control students (PDF p. 9, Participants and Experimental procedure; PDF pp. 11-13, Tables 2-8). The randomized count denotes people in assigned classes; individual students were not independently randomized.
participants.who: Chemistry majors taking the compulsory Modern Educational Technology course at a public normal university; average age 20, with no prior knowledge of designing and developing courseware (PDF p. 9, Participants; PDF p. 15, Limitations and future research).
participants.quote: A total of 81 participants (aged 20 on average) were from two classes
participants.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Participants and Experimental procedure; PDF pp. 11-13 (printed pp. 50-52), Tables 2-8; PDF p. 15 (printed p. 54), Limitations and future research.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, accessed through a locally developed Tencent QQ learning system; underlying model/version not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Learners could address an AI teacher in QQ for continuous personalized questions, answers and guidance before and during class. The system also sent assignment reminders, monitored participation and encouraged critical dialogue. It supplied answers and solutions, so it is not coded as a content-free coach (PDF pp. 5-8, ChatGPT-FLGA and the learning system, Figures 1-6; PDF p. 13, Interview results).

task.description: Design and develop multimedia courseware using Microsoft PowerPoint, including single-choice and flying-centipede animations. The instructional examples invite discussion and creation, but the exact pre- and post-project assessment prompts are not supplied (PDF p. 6, Figures 1-2 and accompanying text; PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure; PDF p. 10, Table 1).
task.duration: The experiment began March 13, 2023: three weeks of introductory instruction, pre-test and questionnaires in week 4, three weeks of assigned learning, and post-test and questionnaires in week 8. Time allowed for producing each assessed project and the exact interval in days from the final AI-supported learning session to assessment are not stated (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

outcomes.name: Post-project courseware performance / quality (creative-task scope unclear)
outcomes.measure_detail: Two experienced educational-technology instructors scored each pre- and post-project; the student score is their average. The rubric has a maximum of 100 and five dimensions: instruction (fit to teaching needs), science (content errors), technology (materials optimization), artistry (appropriate matching of materials), and operability (interface friendliness). Each dimension has printed levels of 5, 10, 15 and 20 points. Only the composite performance outcome is reported; there are no separate dimension results. Coded usefulness because it assesses artifact quality/appropriateness, but the paper does not explicitly score novelty, originality or overall creativity, and does not supply the exact scored task prompt. ANCOVA controls the corresponding pre-project score (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments and Table 1; PDF p. 11, Experimental results and Table 2).
outcomes.delay: Post-test in the later week-8 assessment session, after the three weeks of assigned learning following the week-4 pre-test. Delayed follows the codebook definition of a later session; it does not imply a specified retention interval or AI removal. The exact delay in days and AI access during project production are not stated (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

outcomes.name: Creative thinking tendency (self-report; does not meet the output criterion)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Creative Thinking Tendency Scale from Lai and Hwang (2014): five self-report items, rated from 5 = strongly agree to 1 = strongly disagree; Cronbach’s α = 0.83. Example item: “I like to ask some questions that others do not think of.” This measures reported tendency rather than a score on creative output. ANCOVA controls the pre-questionnaire rating (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments; PDF p. 11, Experimental results; PDF p. 13, Table 8). Retained to document why the paper’s named creativity result cannot establish eligibility. No output construct applies: construct is null because codebook section 6 defines other as an outcome scored on output.
outcomes.delay: Post-questionnaire in the later week-8 assessment session after the three weeks of assigned learning. Delayed follows the codebook definition of a later session; the exact delay in days is not stated. This outcome is self-report and has no scored creative output (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

eligibility.reason: Random assignment of one intact class to ChatGPT guidance is explicit, supporting field_rct with class-level assignment during ordinary coursework despite the author's quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 1 and 9, abstract and Participants). The two analyzed arms contain 42 and 39 students, for the reported total of 81 people; criterion 2 is met (PDF p. 9, Participants and Experimental procedure; PDF pp. 11-13, Tables 2-8). Creative-thinking tendency is a self-report agreement questionnaire, so it has no applicable output construct and cannot satisfy criterion 3 (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments). Instructors scored each student's courseware, and the quality/appropriateness rubric supports the provisional usefulness coding. However, the exact assessed project prompts are absent. Figure 2 permits imitation or creation of new work during learning, without establishing the task used for the scored assessment (PDF p. 6, Figure 2; PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure). The rubric assesses teaching fit, content correctness, materials optimization and matching, and interface friendliness; it does not explicitly score novelty, originality or overall creativity (PDF p. 10, Table 1). Thus artifact scoring is confirmed, but whether the assessed task meets the codebook's open-ended creative-task definition remains unclear. Criterion 3 and core eligibility remain unclear pending assessment instructions from the authors. AI access during production of the scored post-project is also unspecified (PDF pp. 6 and 9). This separate gap determines with_ai versus after_ai; either classification can qualify, so that gap alone does not change the three eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-FLGA had higher adjusted courseware-quality scores (89.93 vs 87.13) and self-reported creative-thinking scores (19.07 vs 17.40), but creative-task scope and AI access during assessment remain unclear (PDF pp. 11 and 13, Tables 2 and 8).
open_questions: What were the exact assessed pre- and post-project prompts, and did they require open-ended creative design rather than reproduction of taught PowerPoint techniques? Without the prompts, the courseware-quality composite cannot be confirmed as a qualifying usefulness outcome (PDF pp. 6, 9-10, Figure 2 and Table 1).

Was ChatGPT available while students produced the scored post-project in week 8? The document establishes access during learning but does not state assessment-period access or withdrawal, so with_ai versus after_ai remains unconfirmed (PDF pp. 6 and 9, learning system and Experimental procedure).
notes: Reconciliation on 2026-10-09. Both raw forms parsed successfully. The complete markdown conversion was read in order, including all references and final publication information; no appendix is present. Eligibility passages and every retained numerical fact were checked against PDF text; Tables 1, 2 and 8 were also checked with PyMuPDF table extraction. Figures 1-4 and 7 were inspected from PDF renders held in memory. There is one comparative intervention study. Preparatory needs interviews involved 10 students and three teachers (PDF p. 5, Instructional design model); follow-up interviews involved six students, three from each experimental arm (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure; PDF p. 13, Interview results). These are not additional intervention samples or additional people added to the 81 analyzed participants. The outcome array retains the candidate artifact-quality composite and the named creativity self-report for explicit exclusion; it does not assert that either is a confirmed eligible creative-output estimate. Self-efficacy, learning attitudes and motivation are omitted because they are not scored on creative output. There is no reported across-person diversity measure or separate rubric-dimension comparison. Assignment was to classes, with one class per arm, and the reported student-level ANCOVA does not describe adjustment for class clustering (PDF pp. 9 and 11). The standard errors in the tables belong to adjusted arm means, not the arm contrast; partial eta squared is the printed effect measure. No effect size or contrast standard error was computed. The project-performance p = 0.00 and adjusted mean 89.93 are retained exactly as printed (PDF p. 11, Table 2 and accompanying prose). Delayed timing follows the codebook's later-session definition because assessment took place in week 8 after the three-week learning phase; no exact delay in days or AI withdrawal is inferred. Figure 7 repeats the label Pre-test and pre-questionnaire in its final box, while the prose explicitly identifies week-8 post-tests and post-questionnaires; coding follows the prose (PDF p. 9). Null question and AI-availability fields preserve the unresolved project-production conditions; the self-report outcome has question none and null AI availability because it is not creative output. The paper does not state a preregistration, primary outcome designation, sample reuse, supplement or data/code availability link. Comparisons covered design, assignment, arms, participants, tool/role, task, outcome inventory and coding, statistics/locators, supplement, sample overlap, company involvement, eligibility and finding. Equivalent wording, alternative supporting locators, reordered statistic-type lists, and complementary subsets of the same results in the one-line summaries are not counted as differences. Blank sample-overlap reporting in A and explicit not-stated reporting in B describe the same absence of a reported link. The seven differences include five substantive numerical omissions as well as the two timing codes. n_unresolved counts distinct outstanding source issues across differences and agreed_fields_checked: all seven A/B differences are resolved, but two agreed eligibility-relevant fields could not be confirmed. These two shared gaps are recorded with confirmed false and repeated in open_questions. Final review on 2026-10-09: all three challenge files were read; only the outcome lens raised a problem. The complete markdown conversion, including references and final publication information, was read. No appendix is present. The challenge passage, eligibility evidence, participant counts and retained study statistics were checked against PDF text; Tables 1, 2 and 8 were also checked with text-based PyMuPDF table extraction. Figures 1, 2 and 7 were inspected in memory. The self-report construct was corrected to null. The existing source.supplement entry is complete and remains not_stated; no supplement or data/code link is identified in the article. All reconciliation.differences are resolved. The two unconfirmed agreed-field entries are covered by final.open_items. The creative-task assessment gap affects criterion 3; AI availability during assessment affects question classification only. This final distinction supersedes the earlier notes' description of both gaps as eligibility-relevant. Challenge counts count dispositions of checker problems, so n_open is zero despite two separate open source questions. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

Retained the questionnaire for explicit exclusion, with measure self_report, scored_on_output false and question none. This correction does not establish eligibility for the separate courseware-quality outcome.

open_items.item: Exact assessed pre- and post-project prompts: whether the rated courseware required open-ended creative design, making its quality/appropriateness score a qualifying usefulness outcome. This determines criterion 3 and core eligibility. The authors would need to provide the assessment instructions and permitted outputs; the learning example in Figure 2 does not establish the scored assessment task (PDF pp. 6, 9-10, Figure 2, Experimental procedure and Table 1). This covers open_questions[0] and the unconfirmed eligibility entry in reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked.

ChatGPT availability while the week-8 scored post-project was produced: the authors would need to clarify whether access continued or was removed during production. This determines with_ai versus after_ai only; either can qualify after randomized AI exposure, so this answer alone does not change an eligibility criterion (PDF pp. 6 and 9, learning-system description and Experimental procedure). This covers open_questions[1] and the unconfirmed AI-availability/question entry in reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked.
